Unit 4: The Why of Motion

Phenomenon: The Construction of the Great Pyramid

Segment 1

20 min

The Weight of a Stone

A. Context: The primary challenge was the immense weight of each stone block. We must first quantify the force of gravity to understand how to move it.

B. Core Practice: A block has a mass of 2.5 metric tons (2500 kg).

  • Calculate the block's weight (Fg = mg).
  • On flat ground, what is the normal force (FN)?
  • How does the normal force relate to the weight?

C. Synthesis (Scale): If a worker pulls with 500 N, what proportion of the block's weight can they support?

D. Metacognition: Why is it crucial to treat weight and normal force as two distinct forces?

Segment 2

20 min

The Struggle Against Friction

A. Context: The Egyptians wet the sand to reduce friction. We will now quantify why this innovation was so critical.

B. Core Practice: Given μs = 0.4 and μk = 0.25.

  • Calculate the max static friction force.
  • Calculate the kinetic friction force.
  • Compare the force needed to start vs. sustain motion.

C. Synthesis (Cause/Effect): How did wetting the sand (the cause) directly impact the workforce needed (the effect)?

D. Metacognition: How does a free-body diagram illustrate friction as a "resistance" force?

Segment 3

20 min

The Challenge of the Ramp

A. Context: Using a ramp changes the problem. Part of the block's weight now pulls it *down* the ramp, working against the builders.

B. Core Practice: A 2500 kg block is on a 10° ramp (ignore friction for now).

  • Sketch the Fg vector and its components.
  • Calculate the perpendicular component (Fg,⊥).
  • Calculate the parallel component (Fg,∥).

C. Synthesis (Systems): How does our new coordinate system (parallel/perpendicular) make the problem easier to analyze?

D. Metacognition: Without calculating, how would the force components change if the ramp angle increased?

Segment 4

20 min

The Force to Haul

A. Context: We can now calculate the total force required to pull the block up the ramp at a constant velocity, balancing all forces.

B. Core Practice: A 2500 kg block is pulled up a 10° ramp (μk = 0.25).

  • Calculate the new Normal Force on the ramp.
  • Calculate the new Friction Force on the ramp.
  • Calculate the total pulling force required.

C. Synthesis (Cause/Effect): What must be true about the net force (the cause) to achieve the effect of constant velocity?

D. Metacognition: Write a plain-language recipe for finding the force to pull an object up any ramp with friction.

Segment 5

20 min

Synthesis: Foreman's Report

A. Context: As a foreman, you must efficiently assign workers to move a block up a ramp, accounting for both starting and sliding friction.

B. Core Practice: A 2500kg block, 10° ramp, μs=0.4, μk=0.25. Each worker pulls with 500 N. Report:

  • Total force to start motion.
  • Total force to sustain motion.
  • Min. workers to start.
  • Min. workers to sustain.

C. Synthesis (Scale): How does the proportion of starting vs. sliding force affect your workforce logistics?

D. Metacognition: What was the single critical difference between the "starting" and "sliding" calculations?

Segment 6

20 min

Metacognition & The Model

A. Context: Our physics model is a powerful but simplified view of the complex, real-world process of building the pyramids.

B. Core Practice: Conceptual Review

  • Explain how a free-body diagram is an essential model.
  • How would a bumpy or dry ramp change the required force?
  • What additional force is needed to accelerate the block?

C. Synthesis (Cause/Effect): State two key cause-and-effect relationships a foreman must understand.

D. Metacognition: What did our model clarify, and what real-world factors (e.g., worker fatigue) did it ignore?
